name: Optimising Lab Protocols
title: Optimising Lab Protocols
answer: Optimising lab protocols uses AI and simulation to refine the sequence, timing, and parameters of experimental procedures. The goal is to reduce wasted reagents, shorten cycle times, and make results more reproducible across runs and sites. This work sits within laboratory automation and simulation, where a protocol is treated as a structured workflow that can be measured, modeled, and improved. It covers wet lab steps such as pipetting, incubation, centrifugation, and plate handling, as well as the data capture that follows.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Optimising lab protocols uses AI and simulation to refine the sequence, timing, and parameters of experimental procedures. The goal is to reduce wasted reagents, shorten cycle times, and make results more reproducible across runs and sites. This work sits within laboratory automation and simulation, where a protocol is treated as a structured workflow that can be measured, modeled, and improved. It covers wet lab steps such as pipetting, incubation, centrifugation, and plate handling, as well as the data capture that follows.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on laboratory automation hardware such as liquid handling robots, robotic arms, plate readers, and environmental control systems. These instruments are connected to scheduling software and, increasingly, to digital twins that mirror the physical setup. Simulation environments let teams test protocol changes without consuming materials or occupying instruments. Compute for model training and inference is typically standard scientific computing infrastructure, with data flowing from instrument logs, sensor readings, and electronic lab notebooks.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners model a protocol as a graph or sequence of operations with adjustable parameters such as volumes, temperatures, and dwell times. Simulation and surrogate models predict outcomes for untested parameter sets, while Bayesian optimisation and active learning choose the next experiments to run. Reinforcement learning is sometimes used to learn control policies for dynamic steps like mixing or liquid transfer. The loop between prediction, physical execution, and measurement is repeated until the protocol meets a defined performance target.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on data provenance, protocol versioning, and the validity of simulated results. Teams need clear records of which protocol version produced which dataset, and whether a result came from a physical run or a simulation. Reproducibility depends on capturing instrument calibration, reagent lot numbers, and environmental conditions alongside the protocol. Risks include overfitting to a single instrument or lab, silent drift in sensors, and the use of simulation results as if they were physical evidence. Provenance systems and audit trails are used to trace every change and its effect.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward closed loop laboratories where AI proposes, runs, and evaluates protocol changes with minimal human intervention. Digital twins are expected to become more accurate and more tightly coupled to physical instruments, allowing faster and safer optimisation. Large language models are being explored for generating protocol drafts from natural language descriptions, though their outputs still require simulation and physical validation. Cross lab standardisation of protocol representations may make it easier to transfer optimised methods between sites without losing performance.
